catalog_quote: In this study we present the basics of tone in the Thɔnkɔ /t̪ɔ́nkɔ́/ dialect. We will show that when H(igh) tones become L(ow) tones by rule, they still stick around as “traces” on their respective TBUs. ... In Thɔnkɔ dialect of Limba, with two exceptions (see (3) below), words end with a L tone. Out of 504 nouns in our current lexicon, 403 are all L(ow) in their citation form. Examples are seen in (1a), where the lack of an acute accent on a vowel indicates L tone ... These alternations show that there is a process which lowers an underlying H or sequence of H tones before pause. As expressed informally in (2), we propose that the trigger of lowering is a final L% boundary tone. ... The lowering process in (2) affects all word classes: nouns, verbs, adjectives, numerals, determiners etc. The only exceptions we have found are the three grammatical words in (3). ... We thus have an opaque tone system: Words pronounced in isolation tell you almost nothing about their underlying tones. [BPFL pp. 2-3] ... Concerning the tone system, Limba-Thɔnkɔ contrasts H and L, as well as a derived downstep (ꜜ) occurring before some instances of H. H is marked by an acute accent, while L is unmarked, e.g. H-L kóma ‘grandson’. [LLA p. 4]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Both first-hand descriptions treat Thɔnkɔ Limba as a two-tone (H/L, plus downstep) language whose H tones are lowered before pause, so that most words are all-low in citation form and underlying tones surface only in context. Neither paper says anything about word stress, accent or prominence: no rule for stress placement is given and no claim that stress is absent is made.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal only: two exception classes to word-final L (their (3)); 97 of 504 nouns end in a H͡L fall or H.L sequence that survives in isolation. Nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone in citation form vs. in phrasal context (noun + determiner, verb phrase, clause); Final High Lowering is triggered by an utterance-final L% boundary tone (declaratives, imperatives, yes-no questions, not WH questions). Data are elicited from one speaker (D. I. Kamara, Kabasa village, Kambia District).
new_statements.identity_note: The two saved first-hand descriptions are of the Thɔnkɔ (Tonko) dialect (Kabasa village, Kambia District, western Limba area). Glottolog's reference record equates 'Thɔnkɔ = Thonko-Sela = West Limba' with West-Central Limba [lia] (west2450), whose listed dialects are Central [cent2017] and Western Limba [west2451]; Thɔnkɔ-Sɛla corresponds to the western branch (west2451). The older literature (Clarke 1922, and Mukarovsky 1962/63 which draws on it) describes Biriwa-Safrɔkɔ, which Glottolog files under East Limba [lma, east2387], so those works would not settle west2450 even if opened.
